title: Boolean decision-Holant dichotomy
formal:
Classify the polynomial-time solvable Boolean decision-Holant problems for all fixed finite families of Boolean relations. More precisely, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), determine the entire characteristic function
\[\chi_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal F)=\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\in\mathrm P,\\0,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\notin\mathrm P,\end{cases}\]
with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite family \(\mathcal F\). The answer must give a substantive structural criterion on the allowed relations, with algorithms and complementary lower bounds, rather than merely restating the definition of polynomial-time solvability. The model is the source’s Boolean edge-CSP interpretation of decision Holant, specified below.
why: A full classification would explain exactly which local Boolean constraints remain tractable when each variable has two incidences. The unresolved region contains broad generalizations of matching rather than only the standard Boolean CSP algorithms. Resolving it would connect delta-matroid structure with the boundary between polynomial-time graph algorithms and NP-hardness.
status_note: The 2017 survey explicitly leaves the general Boolean decision-Holant classification open. The checked 2023 ISAAC paper, §1 p. 57:4, explicitly retains that question and the all-delta-matroids tractability conjecture. Bounded primary-source searches on 16 September 2026 found later special-case and counting results but no matching full decision classification; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness. The finite-family tractability characteristic function, P≠NP convention and loopless edge-CSP input model are explicit editorial specifications grounded in the cited sources.

sentences: Boolean decision Holant asks whether edges of a graph can be assigned zero or one so that every local relation is satisfied.
The question seeks a structural classification of all fixed finite relation families that admit polynomial-time decision.
The source’s edge-CSP model makes each variable occur in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without freely adding constants or unary relations.
Known results handle the non-delta-matroid boundary, symmetric delta-matroids and even delta-matroids, while the arbitrary delta-matroid region remains the general obstacle.
A complete answer would identify the full tractability boundary beyond ordinary Boolean CSP and matching.

definitions:
A Boolean relation of arity \(r\geq1\) is a subset \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), equivalently its zero-one indicator function \(f_R\). A signature family \(\mathcal F\) is a finite ordered list of such relations given by their full finite truth tables; empty relations and the empty family are allowed. For each decision problem the family and all arities are fixed before inputs are supplied. Arbitrarily large fixed arities are covered across the classification.

A signature grid is a finite undirected loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), together with a label \(R_v\in\mathcal F\) at each vertex and an ordering \((e_{v,1},\ldots,e_{v,r_v})\) of its incident edges, where \(r_v\) equals the arity of \(R_v\). Parallel edges are permitted and are separate variables. The graph need not be planar or bipartite. Each edge has two distinct endpoints and appears exactly once at each endpoint. The incidence order is part of the input, since relations need not be symmetric. This is the explicit convention of Definitions 1–3 in the cited edge-CSP paper: a variable is in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without a repeated coordinate within one scope.

A Boolean assignment is a map \(\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}\). It is satisfying when \((\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v}))\in R_v\) for every vertex. Define
\[H_{\mathcal F}(G)=\sum_{\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}}\prod_{v\in V} f_{R_v}(\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v})).\]
The task \(\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\) accepts exactly the grids with \(H_{\mathcal F}(G)>0\). It asks for one yes/no answer, not the number or a list of satisfying assignments. The empty graph has value one, by the empty-product convention. A grid containing an empty relation is unsatisfiable. Nullary indicators, if included, can be processed separately: zero rejects the instance and one is deleted, so restricting the signature tables to positive arities loses no tractability class.

Encode the numbers of vertices and edges in unary; list binary endpoint indices for each numbered edge, the fixed-family index at each vertex, and its ordered list of edge indices. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Validity of the encoding is checked in polynomial time; malformed strings are rejected. A polynomial-time algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts with the correct answer on every input in at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps, for positive constants \(C,k\) depending on \(\mathcal F\). There is no randomness, oracle or advice. Programs may depend on the fixed family, and no common running-time exponent across all families is requested.

No unary relation, pinning constant, equality relation, edge weight or graph restriction is freely added to \(\mathcal F\). The at-most-two-occurrences decision model used in the survey has the same complexity under this scope convention: remove unused variables, take two copies of the instance, and identify corresponding variables that occurred only once. This gives exactly two occurrences and preserves satisfiability without new relations. The target does not impose a uniform input-template algorithm or require a polynomial-time procedure for recognizing the tractable families from their truth tables.

Here \(\mathrm P\) is deterministic polynomial time and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages whose membership has polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. Every fixed-family problem above is in NP, with the edge assignment as certificate. NP-hardness, when used in the classification, means deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions from every language in NP; NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP. This is an explicit reduction convention. The separation assumption makes a tractability classification nontrivial; if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the function is identically one. A rational answer within \(1/100\) of a zero-one value determines that value, but the requested result is the structural description of the whole function, not numerical experiments on selected families.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of an exhaustive structural characterization of \(\chi_{\mathrm H}\) with the stated absolute \(1/100\) accuracy, under the explicit \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis. Prove correct polynomial-time decision algorithms for every family assigned one and a matching exclusion of polynomial time for every family assigned zero; NP-hardness under the stated reductions is a sufficient exclusion. The result must cover all finite Boolean signature families, including arbitrary delta-matroid relations, with the graph and occurrence conventions above. A characterization cannot simply rename the existence of a polynomial-time machine. Classifying only symmetric signatures, only even delta-matroids, planar inputs, weighted counting, or a language enlarged by freely available unary signatures does not answer the full question. If additional complexity cases arise instead of the expected polynomial-time/NP-complete dichotomy, identify and justify them rather than asserting that every nontractable case is NP-complete without proof.

source_formulation.text: Classify Boolean decision-Holant problems; the remaining general obstacle is the complexity of delta-matroid relations.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of §3. The complete fixed-finite-family tractability target, conditional separation convention and cited loopless edge-CSP model are explicit.

context_blocks.text: In ordinary CSP a variable may constrain many locations. In a Holant grid each variable is an edge linking two local constraints. This restriction creates new algorithms: an ExactOne relation accepts precisely tuples with one coordinate equal to one, and using it at every vertex asks for a perfect matching. Thus tractability is not exhausted by the familiar Boolean CSP cases.

For a nonempty relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), the delta-matroid exchange property says: if \(x,y\in R\) differ at coordinate \(i\), then either flipping \(i\) in \(x\) stays in \(R\), or there is a different coordinate \(j\) at which \(x,y\) differ such that flipping both \(i,j\) stays in \(R\). An even delta-matroid additionally has the same parity of Hamming weight for all its tuples; that parity may be odd. Empty relations are handled separately by immediate rejection when used.

The source’s Theorem 8 records Feder’s boundary: if a family contains a relation failing the delta-matroid exchange property, its decision-Holant complexity agrees with that of ordinary CSP on the family. Schaefer’s Boolean CSP dichotomy then supplies a polynomial-time algorithm or NP-completeness. The remaining general region consists of families whose relations all satisfy the exchange property.

For symmetric relations, membership depends only on the number of one coordinates. The delta-matroid condition then says that between consecutive permitted weights there is at most one forbidden integer. Such families are tractable as general factor problems. This permits relations with both parities; it is a different sufficient condition from the even delta-matroid algorithm.

Kazda, Kolmogorov and Rolínek generalize the matching blossom algorithm to arbitrary even delta-matroid relations given by tuple lists, and extend it to a further class they call efficiently coverable. Their planar Boolean CSP classification is a consequence. It does not classify arbitrary delta-matroid constraints in general edge-CSP grids.

The 2023 general-factor paper explicitly retains the general Boolean edge-CSP classification as open, while proving a strongly polynomial algorithm for particular weighted symmetric constraints. It records the conjecture that every delta-matroid family is tractable. The card retains the full classification question, so it does not assume this conjectured answer in its target.

A counting dichotomy concerns computing the entire sum H, which can be harder than deciding whether H is positive. Counting Holant results for real or complex signatures therefore cannot by themselves classify this zero-one decision task. Availability of all unary signatures and restrictions to planar grids also define different problems.
